To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
highly glycated human oxy-haemoglobin, at concentrations that occur physiologically in the blood of diabetic patients, impairs nitro oxide-mediated responses by generating superoxide radicals.
glycated human oxyhemoglobin, at physiological concentrations, impairs the nitric oxide-dependent vasodilator responses by a mechanism that involves superoxide anions.
highly glycated human haemo-globin impairs endothelium-dependent nitric oxide relax-ations in human mesentery microvessels by generation of superoxide anions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the mechanisms by which glycated proteins induce endothelial dysfunction.
the study of the effects of glycated haemoglobin on vascular function, and with the identification of the mechanisms involved.
the role of the vascular endothelium in the pathogenesis of diabetic microangiopathy, and the mechanisms involved in the endothelial dysfunction observed in diabetes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
glycated haemoglobin impairs NO-mediated relaxations in human vessels by generating superoxides, which in turn, inhibit the NO-mediated relaxations.

glycated haemoglobin (glycohaemoglobin), at physiological plasmalitic concentrations, impairs endothelium-dependent relaxation by inhibiting the production of nitric oxide, and this impairment is mediated by superoxide anions.
glycated haemoglobin impairs endothelial function by inhibiting the production of nitric oxide, which in turn leads to a decrease in blood flow to the tissues.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the high levels of glycated hemoglobin (HbA(1c)) in diabetes mellitus can cause endothelial dysfunction by generating superoxide radicals that interfere with the nitric oxide-mediated relaxation of blood vessels.
glycated haemoglobin impairs NO-mediated relaxations in human microvessels.

the glycated haemoglobin impairs the nitric oxide relaxant response in human mesentric microvessels, and this effect is due to the generation of superoxide anion, which in turn is prevented by the addition of superoxide dismutate.
The main takeaway from our work is that

highly glycated human oxyhemoglobin, at physiological plasma concentrations, impairs the relaxation induced by nitric oxide in human mesenterial microvessels, a mechanism involving superoxides but not cyclooxygenses.
highly glycated oxyhaemboglobin, at physiological concentrations, can impair endothelial-dependent relaxations by a mechanism involving the generation of superoxide anions.
glycated haemoglobin can cause vascular dysfunction in humans.
